questions.q: All GraphQL operations are sent to the same endpoint.
questions.explain: Unlike REST, which uses operation-specific endpoints across a range of HTTP methods, every GraphQL operation uses a single endpoint.

questions.q: What determines how a GraphQL request is handled?
choices: The endpoint path it is sent to
The type and name of the operation
questions.explain: With GraphQL the type and name of the operation define how the query is handled, rather than the endpoint it is sent to or the HTTP method used.

questions.q: Which of the following are the operation types used to manipulate data described by a GraphQL schema?
questions.explain: Queries fetch data, mutations add/change/remove data, and subscriptions set up a permanent connection by which the server pushes data to the client.

questions.q: Which GraphQL operation type adds, changes, or removes data (roughly equivalent to REST's POST, PUT, and DELETE)?
questions.explain: Mutations change data in some way. They always take an input of some type, generally provided as a variable.

questions.q: GraphQL lets a client specify exactly what data it wants, helping to avoid which problem common with REST APIs?
choices: Large response objects and multiple calls
questions.explain: By specifying exactly what data it wants, the client avoids the large response objects and multiple calls that can be seen with REST APIs.

questions.q: In a GraphQL schema definition, what does the `!` operator after a field's type indicate?
questions.explain: The `!` operator indicates that the field is non-nullable when called, that is, mandatory.

questions.q: A GraphQL schema must include at least one available query.
questions.explain: Schemas must include at least one available query, and usually also contain details of available mutations.

questions.q: Most of the types defined in a GraphQL schema are which kind of type?
questions.explain: Most of the types defined are object types, which define the objects available and the fields and arguments they have.

questions.q: What is the name for the contract between the frontend and backend that defines the available data as a series of types using a human-readable definition language?
questions.explain: The schema defines the structure of the service's data, listing the available types, fields, and relationships.

questions.q: What problem do aliases solve in a GraphQL query?
choices: They allow returning multiple instances of the same object type in one request
questions.explain: GraphQL objects can't contain multiple properties with the same name; aliases bypass this by explicitly naming the properties, letting you return multiple instances of the same type in one request.

questions.q: Without using aliases, a single GraphQL query can contain multiple properties with the same name.
questions.explain: Ordinarily GraphQL objects can't contain multiple properties with the same name, which is exactly the restriction aliases work around.

questions.q: What is a GraphQL fragment?
choices: A reusable part of a query or mutation containing a subset of a type's fields
A fragment of the schema exposed by introspection
A malformed query that triggers an error
questions.explain: Fragments are reusable parts of queries or mutations that contain a subset of the fields belonging to the associated type; changing a fragment updates every query that calls it.

questions.q: What do GraphQL variables enable you to do?
choices: Pass dynamic arguments instead of embedding them directly in the query string
Combine queries and mutations into one operation type
questions.explain: Variables let you pass dynamic arguments from a separate JSON variables dictionary, so a common query structure can be reused with only the variable value changing.

questions.q: Using aliases with mutations effectively enables an attacker to do what?
choices: Send multiple GraphQL messages in a single HTTP request
questions.explain: Aliases with mutations let you send multiple GraphQL messages in one HTTP request, which can be used to bypass request-count-based rate limiting.

questions.q: Which query component, if user-supplied and used to access objects directly, can make a GraphQL API vulnerable to IDOR?
questions.explain: If user-supplied arguments are used to access objects directly, the API can be vulnerable to access control issues such as insecure direct object references (IDOR).

questions.q: How are GraphQL subscriptions commonly implemented?
questions.explain: Subscriptions establish a long-lived connection so the server can push real-time updates, and are commonly implemented using WebSockets.

questions.q: What universal query can you send to probe whether a URL corresponds to a GraphQL service?
questions.explain: Sending query{__typename} to a GraphQL endpoint returns the string {"data": {"__typename": "query"}} somewhere in the response.

questions.q: Why does the universal query work on any GraphQL endpoint?
choices: Every endpoint has a reserved __typename field that returns the queried object's type as a string
Every endpoint leaks its schema by default
questions.explain: Every GraphQL endpoint has a reserved field called __typename that returns the queried object's type as a string.

questions.q: Which of these are common GraphQL endpoint suffixes worth probing with a universal query?
questions.explain: Common suffixes include /graphql, /api, /api/graphql, /graphql/api, and /graphql/graphql; you can also try appending /v1.

questions.q: As best practice, what should a production GraphQL endpoint accept to help protect against CSRF?
choices: Only POST requests with a content-type of application/json
Any method with a content-type of x-www-form-urlencoded
questions.explain: Best practice is for production endpoints to only accept POST requests with a content-type of application/json, which helps protect against CSRF.

questions.q: If common GraphQL endpoint paths don't return a GraphQL response, what short path segment does the material suggest appending to try?
questions.explain: If the common endpoints don't return a GraphQL response, you could also try appending /v1 to the path.

questions.q: Best practice is for introspection to be enabled in production environments.
questions.explain: It is best practice for introspection to be disabled in production, as it can disclose sensitive data and help an attacker learn how to interact with the API.

questions.q: Which field do you query to use introspection to discover schema information?
questions.explain: To use introspection, query the __schema field, which is available on the root type of all queries.

questions.q: Name the tool that uses suggestions to automatically recover all or part of a GraphQL schema even when introspection is disabled.
questions.explain: Clairvoyance uses suggestion responses to piece together the schema, even when introspection is turned off.

questions.q: Suggestions, which can reveal valid parts of the schema in error messages, are a feature of which platform?
questions.explain: Suggestions are an Apollo GraphQL feature where the server suggests query amendments (for example, 'Did you mean...') in error messages, effectively giving away valid schema parts.

questions.q: To bypass a flawed regex that blocks the string `__schema{`, which characters can you insert after `__schema` because GraphQL ignores them but the regex may not?
questions.explain: Spaces, new lines, and commas are ignored by GraphQL but not by a flawed regex, so inserting one after __schema can defeat a regex that only excludes '__schema{'.

questions.q: If an introspection probe is blocked over POST, what else should you try?
choices: Resending it over an alternative method such as GET or POST with x-www-form-urlencoded
questions.explain: Introspection may only be disabled over POST, so try a GET request or a POST with a content-type of x-www-form-urlencoded.

questions.q: Retrieving a delisted product by directly supplying its sequential ID to a query is an example of what vulnerability class?
choices: An access control vulnerability / insecure direct object reference (IDOR)
questions.explain: If arguments are used to access objects directly, a user can obtain data they shouldn't by supplying a matching argument, which is an access control issue known as IDOR.

questions.q: How can aliases be used to bypass rate limiting?
choices: They make the server forget previous requests
They let many queries ride in one HTTP request, defeating limiters that count HTTP requests rather than operations
They disable the rate limiter in the schema
They spoof the client's IP address
questions.explain: Some rate limiters count HTTP requests instead of operations performed; because aliases send multiple queries in a single HTTP message, they can bypass such limits (for example, brute forcing discount codes).

questions.q: Under what conditions does a CSRF-over-GraphQL vulnerability arise?
choices: When the endpoint does not validate the content type of requests and no CSRF tokens are implemented
When the schema exposes a mutation
questions.explain: GraphQL CSRF can arise where the endpoint does not validate request content type and no CSRF tokens are implemented, letting a browser send a forged GET or x-www-form-urlencoded request.

questions.q: A POST request with a content type of application/json is secure against forgery as long as the content type is validated.
questions.explain: A browser can't be made to send a cross-site application/json POST, so if the endpoint validates that content type, such requests are secure against CSRF.

questions.q: Which design steps help defend a GraphQL API against brute force and DoS attacks?
choices: Configure operation limits (max unique fields, aliases, and root fields)
Configure the maximum number of bytes a query can contain
Expose private user fields for faster lookups
questions.explain: Limiting query depth, configuring operation limits, capping query bytes, and implementing cost analysis all reduce the opportunity for brute force and DoS attacks.

questions.q: What does the term 'query depth' refer to?
choices: The number of aliases in a query
The number of levels of nesting within a query
The byte size of a query
questions.explain: Query depth is the number of levels of nesting within a query; heavily nested queries can hurt performance and enable DoS, so limiting depth helps.

questions.q: Which measures specifically defend against GraphQL CSRF?
choices: Only accept queries over JSON-encoded POST
Validate that the provided content matches the supplied content type
Implement a secure CSRF token mechanism
Accept GET requests for all operations
questions.explain: To defend against GraphQL CSRF, accept queries only over JSON-encoded POST, validate the content matches the content type, and use a secure CSRF token mechanism.

questions.q: What does cost analysis do for a GraphQL API?
choices: Identifies the resource cost of incoming queries and drops ones too computationally complex to run
Measures the monetary cost of hosting
questions.explain: Cost analysis has a library identify the resource cost of queries as they arrive and drop any query that would be too computationally complex to run.
